prompt.context: Your client designs, manufactures, and markets a full line of bicycles. The company's sales and profits had been growing until three years ago when its profitability flattened and began declining.
prompt.question: Why did profitability decline and how can the client fix the problem?

clarifying_info.q: Have revenues been growing or declining?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues are growing roughly at the same rate as before the downturn.
Expenses are increasing disproportionately relative to revenues.

clarifying_info.q: Are cost increases driven by operating or administrative activities?
clarifying_info.a: Administrative costs are growing, but operating costs account for the bulk of increased expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Are fixed or variable costs driving the increase in operating costs?
clarifying_info.a: Fixed costs are growing but variable costs appear to account for the bulk of increased expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Within variable costs, are direct or indirect costs increasing more?
clarifying_info.a: Both have been growing. Bicycles have become more sophisticated with better materials and components. However, the increasing cost per bike has been comparable to the growing price per bike. Indirect costs are increasing disproportionately.

clarifying_info.q: Within indirect variable costs, are materials or labor the bigger driver?
clarifying_info.a: Allocations of indirect materials are about the same. Allocation of indirect labor appears to be the big problem.

clarifying_info.q: Why are indirect labor costs increasing — are there bottlenecks? Has work-in-progress inventory increased?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, WIP inventory has increased. When you look at the factory floor, you see many bikes waiting around.
No, it is not capacity related — there is plenty of throughput available. However, much time is spent in setup activities: resetting paint booths, welding jigs, dies and presses, etc.
No, it has actually decreased as the workforce has improved setup tools, jigs, etc. Workforce turnover and labor relations are all fine.

framework: Start with the profit equation: Profit = (Price × Volume) – Costs
Determine whether the issue is revenue-side or cost-side
Decompose operating costs: fixed vs. variable
Decompose variable costs: direct vs. indirect
Decompose indirect variable costs: materials vs. labor
Identify root cause of indirect labor increase: bottlenecks, setup time, or other
Formulate recommendations to address root cause

questions.prompt: Are revenues or costs driving the profit decline?
questions.guidance: Revenues are growing at the historical rate, so the issue is cost-driven. Candidate should confirm this before moving into cost structure.

questions.prompt: Which cost category is the primary driver of increased expenses?
questions.guidance: Administrative costs are rising but operating costs are the dominant driver. Candidate should narrow focus to operating costs.

questions.prompt: Within operating costs, what is growing — fixed or variable?
questions.guidance: Both are growing, but variable costs are the main culprit. Candidate should drill into variable cost components.

questions.prompt: Within variable costs, what is growing — direct or indirect?
questions.guidance: Direct costs have risen in line with revenue (better materials/components match higher selling price), so the net margin impact is neutral. Indirect costs are rising disproportionately — candidate must focus here.

questions.prompt: Within indirect variable costs, is the driver materials or labor?
questions.guidance: Indirect materials usage per bike is unchanged. Indirect labor is the primary driver — candidate should probe why indirect labor time has increased.

questions.prompt: What is causing indirect labor costs to rise?
questions.guidance: Indirect labor is rising because laborers are spending more time on non-direct activities. Candidate should hypothesize bottlenecks or idle time and ask about WIP inventory. WIP inventory has indeed increased, confirming bottlenecks exist on the factory floor.

Not capacity constraints — throughput capacity is sufficient. The root cause is increased setup time in aggregate: resetting paint booths, welding jigs, dies and presses, etc. Candidate should ask whether time per setup or number of setups has increased.

questions.prompt: Is the increase in setup time due to more time per setup or more setups?
questions.guidance: Time per setup has actually decreased (workforce improvements). Therefore the number of setups has increased. This is because the company proliferated product lines in response to industry trends toward specialization (touring, mountain, racing, hybrid, etc.), creating more SKU variety and smaller production runs per model.

questions.prompt: What can the company do to fix the problem?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) Rationalize/prune the product line to reduce SKU count and number of setups; (2) Increase commonality of components across model lines to reduce setup changes; (3) Increase batch sizes/volume per production run to spread setup costs; (4) Re-examine pricing to reflect true cost of low-volume SKUs.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some things the company can do to alleviate the problem of increasing setups and rising indirect labor costs?

categories.name: Product line rationalization
ideas: Consolidate overlapping models (e.g., merge similar touring variants)
Conduct SKU profitability analysis to identify loss-making lines

categories.name: Component standardization
ideas: Increase shared components across model lines to reduce setup changeovers
Design platforms that support multiple models with minimal retooling
Negotiate with suppliers for standardized parts across SKUs

categories.name: Manufacturing / operations
ideas: Increase production run batch sizes to spread fixed setup costs over more units
Schedule similar models in sequence to minimize setup time between runs
Implement lean/SMED techniques to further reduce setup time

categories.name: Pricing / commercial
ideas: Re-price complex low-volume models to reflect true manufacturing cost
Introduce surcharges or minimum order quantities for customized variants
Shift custom/niche models to a build-to-order model

recommendation: The primary driver of declining profitability is a disproportionate rise in indirect labor costs caused by an increased number of manufacturing setups, which in turn resulted from rapid product line proliferation in response to industry specialization trends.

The client should rationalize its product portfolio by pruning low-volume, low-margin SKUs; standardize components across model lines to reduce changeover frequency; and increase batch sizes per production run to spread setup costs.
risks: Pruning product lines may cede niche market segments to competitors
Component standardization may reduce differentiation and perceived quality in premium segments
Batch size increases may raise finished-goods inventory and working capital requirements
next_steps: Conduct SKU-level profitability analysis to identify which models to cut or reprice
Map component overlap across models to identify standardization opportunities
Model the inventory and cash-flow impact of larger production batches
